title: Neutral atom quantum computing
abstract: Neutral atom qubits are one of the leading approaches for implementation of a large scale quantum computer. The original proposals for neutral atom qubits were formulated more than 25 years ago, with first demonstrations of a universal gate set following 10 years later. In the last few years the performance and scale of neutral atom qubit arrays has developed at a rapid pace leading to demonstrations of quantum algorithms, and logical qubits for fault tolerant error correction. This contribution reviews the physics of the neutral atom approach, surveys current capabilities, and provides an outlook for future progress.
summary: This review surveys the rapidly advancing field of neutral atom quantum computing, establishing it as a leading platform for scalable quantum computation. It details the underlying physics, including trapping methods and Rydberg-mediated entanglement, and reviews current achievements like quantum algorithm demonstrations and logical qubit implementation. The paper serves as a crucial guide for researchers entering or advancing in this complex area.
main_problem: The paper reviews the physics and current state-of-the-art for using neutral atoms as a leading platform for building large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_result: Neutral atom arrays have rapidly advanced, enabling demonstrations of quantum algorithms and the implementation of logical qubits for error correction.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical models of light-atom interactions, trapping mechanisms, and quantum gate operations based on Rydberg physics.
model_or_system: The system involves neutral atoms (like Rb, Cs, Sr, Yb) trapped using far-detuned optical tweezers or lattices. Quantum operations rely on superposition, entanglement, and controlled interactions mediated by Rydberg blockade.
key_observables: Qubit states, entanglement fidelity, coherence time, and the efficiency of quantum gates (e.g., CNOT).
important_parameters: Detuning ($\Delta$), Rabi frequency ($\Omega$), trap confinement strength, and temperature ($k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The review synthesizes results from various models, including those assuming specific ground state energy shifts and the applicability of the Rotating Wave Approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the level structure and relevant transitions for different alkali and alkaline earth atoms, detailing wavelengths used for various processes like cooling and Rydberg excitation.
paper_structure: The paper follows a review structure, covering the fundamental physics, surveying current experimental capabilities, and providing an outlook on future progress in the field.
why_interesting: It provides a comprehensive overview of the physical principles (Rydberg interactions, trapping potentials) and computational milestones (logical qubits, error correction) that bridge AMO physics into the domain of quantum computation.

Figure 2: Level diagrams and often used wavelengths in nm for Sr and Yb atoms. For Sr the wavelength dependent functions are: cooling (461, 689), clock transitions (671, 698), repumpers (448, 679, 707, 483, 497), Rydberg excitation (317, 319, 324). For Yb: cooling (399,556), clock transitions (507,578), repumpers (649,770), Raman transitions (649,770), Rydberg excitation (302, 308, 326). In addition a range of wavelengths are used for trapping and atom transport.

Figure 3: Demonstrations of large qubit arrays. 87Rb: Nearly defect free square array with 2024 atoms in 2025 sites (Lin et al. (2025)); 133Cs: averaged image of atoms in a 12,001 site array (Manetsch et al. (2025)); 88Sr: more than 1000 atoms loaded into an optical lattice (Gyger et al. (2024)); 171Yb: 1225 site array with 99% filling fraction loaded from a reservoir (Norcia et al. (2024)).

Figure 4: Qubit encodings in alkali and AEL atoms. The qubit transitions are indicated with gray arrows with the omg choices labeled for Sr and Yb. Rb and Cs use mf = 0 clock states that have no linear sensitivity to magnetic fields and a weak quadratic sensitivity. In Sr and Yb there are several omg choices for encoding. We may use nuclear spin states in the electronic ground or metastable levels with MF a half integer, and which have small linear Zeeman shifts. Alternatively an optical transition between ground and metstable levels can be used.

Figure 5: Qubit state measurement error for a high background case rb/r1 = 0.1 (left) and a low background case rb/r1 = 0.01 (right). The plots are for |c0|2 = |c1|2 = 1/2 and the curves are labeled with nc. The mean number of detector counts for an atom in the bright state is r1t.
